text: Welcome to Data Governance Program Management. Foundations covered what governance is — this course covers how you actually launch and run a program. We start with the one document that makes a governance effort real: the program charter.

A program charter is the formal document that authorizes a governance program to exist. It names the purpose, the scope, the sponsor, and the success criteria — so when someone asks "who said we could do this," there's a real answer. Without one, governance is just good intentions that any reorg can quietly cancel.

The most common governance failure isn't bad policy — it's scope that tries to cover everything at once. A charter that says "govern all enterprise data" gives you no way to ever say you succeeded. The fix is a phased scope: name two or three high-value domains for phase one, and write down, explicitly, what's out of scope for now.

The executive sponsor and program lead draft the charter together — sponsor brings authority, program lead brings detail. The governance council or committee formally approves it. A charter nobody with real authority signed off on carries no more weight than an email.
Next lesson: once the charter names the scope, you need to know exactly who's affected by it — a full stakeholder identification and analysis.
